talks.title: If You Like It  Put a Ring Signature on It
talks.teaser: The past year has seen excellent research focused on achieving better functionality, privacy, and efficiency for spend obfuscation in digital assets like Monero. This includes CLSAG, DLSAG, Lelantus, Omniring, RingCT ...
talks.summary:
In this cryptographic deep dive at the DEF CON 27 Monero Village, Sarang Noether, Ph.D. from the Monero Research Lab (MRL) analyzes the mathematics and performance characteristics of zero-knowledge ring signatures used to protect transaction privacy in Monero. He begins at 05:00 by addressing the fundamental engineering tradeoffs between cryptographic proof size, signature verification latency, and computational scalability on the blockchain, citing historical challenges faced by privacy protocols.

Dr. Noether explores the mechanics of linkable ring signatures at 10:00, explaining how ring signatures obscure the true signer among decoy outputs while simultaneously using key images to prevent double-spending and balance proof verification to ensure no coins are created out of thin air. At 15:00, he examines emerging cryptographic constructions such as RCT3 and Lelantus, discussing the requirements and trust assumptions involved in potential migration paths for consensus protocols.

At 20:00, he compares the performance and mathematical structure of CLSAG (Compact Linkable Spontaneous Anonymous Group) against DLSAG and Omniring, demonstrating how CLSAG significantly reduces transaction size and verification overhead compared to older MLSAG schemes. He discusses anonymity set scaling and the challenges of batch signature verification at 25:00, concluding at 30:00 with the Monero Research Lab's future roadmap for post-quantum considerations and high-efficiency privacy primitives. talks.title: Perspective of Privacy Blockchain as a Boundary Object
talks.teaser: This talk presents the methodology, findings and conclusions of a boundary theory based Information Systems research project completed at University College Cork, Ireland. Perspectives of privacy have been analyzed fr...
talks.summary:
Dr. Robin Renwick presents findings from an Information Systems research project completed at University College Cork investigating sociotechnical perspectives on privacy within decentralized blockchain networks. Using the framework of Boundary Theory and Susan Leigh Star's concept of "Boundary Objects," Renwick explores how blockchain systems serve as common artifacts that disparate social groups interpret and utilize according to their own values.

[04:36] The study gathers empirical qualitative data through extensive interviews across five key "social worlds" in the blockchain ecosystem: end-users, core cryptographers/developers, corporate/enterprise participants, financial regulators, and legal authorities. Renwick examines the fundamental tensions that emerge between these groups, particularly the ideological view of blockchain as an instrument of decentralized financial sovereignty versus institutional demands for regulatory compliance, AML/KYC enforcement, and systemic transparency.

[11:32] Renwick analyzes how differing definitions of privacy influence architectural decisions, contrasting communities that advocate for mandatory protocol-level privacy (such as Monero) with enterprise or regulatory preferences for selective, opt-in disclosure or "two-tier" privacy models. The talk concludes by emphasizing the importance of understanding these divergent mental models to anticipate regulatory challenges and foster constructive governance dialogues between open-source privacy advocates and external institutions.

talks.title: Improving Monero Release Schedule
talks.teaser: Monero has a biannual major release schedule, but it has been hit with setback after setback despite the best efforts of the community. Justin will discuss how borrowing small changes from other projects to work smart...
talks.summary:
In this talk at the DEF CON 27 Monero Village, Justin Ehrenhofer discusses the governance, software engineering lifecycle, and release coordination challenges within the decentralized Monero project. He opens at 05:00 by reviewing the history of Monero's scheduled hard forks and network upgrades, examining both the successes of regular scheduled upgrades and the logistical friction they create across the broader cryptocurrency ecosystem.

Justin presents key case studies at 10:00, notably the community debate surrounding the deprecation of long, unencrypted payment IDs in favor of subaddresses and integrated addresses, and the coordination required during emergency proof-of-work algorithm modifications against ASICs. At 15:00, he describes the operational strains that biannual network upgrades impose on cryptocurrency exchanges, mining pools, merchant processors, and third-party hardware wallet vendors who must frequently update their infrastructures.

At 20:00, Justin outlines a structured framework to reduce release friction by decoupling routine software maintenance releases (GUI and CLI bug fixes) from consensus-breaking hard forks. He proposes concrete milestones for future release planning at 25:00, advocating for longer feature freezes and predictable testing cycles on testnet and stagenet. He closes at 30:00 by taking audience questions and facilitating an open community discussion on standardizing Monero's release management policies. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Houston we have a problem 86R HB 4371 is a no go video
talks.teaser: A Texas bill has been introduced that encourages the use of what is termed a “verified identity digital currency,” which is a currency that allows the true identities of the sender and the receiver to be known. In add...
talks.summary:
AJ Santos, Assistant Professor at Ankara University, examines Texas House Bill 86R HB 4371 and its implications for cryptocurrency regulation, financial privacy, and decentralized protocols. The proposed legislation sought to regulate cryptocurrency transactions by requiring the recipient of digital funds to verify the identity of the sender, explicitly promoting "verified identity digital currency" while disincentivizing privacy-centric cryptocurrencies such as Monero.

[04:16] Santos dissects the statutory definitions of "money," "currency," and "monetary value" under existing Texas law, focusing on the Texas Money Services Act and guidance issued by the Texas Department of Banking. He highlights legal ambiguities where statutory provisions define currency strictly as coin and paper money authorized by a sovereign government, creating contradictions when lawmakers attempt to regulate decentralized cryptographic tokens under traditional money transmission statutes.

[11:58] The presentation provides comparative legal context by examining Florida case law (such as State v. Espinoza) and federal FinCEN regulatory frameworks regarding money transmitters. Santos identifies major structural flaws in HB 4371, illustrating how reactionary drafting without clear technical comprehension yields unenforceable requirements that conflict with the peer-to-peer mechanics of permissionless blockchains. He concludes by assessing the bill's legislative prospects and discussing how state-level legal definitions shape the broader regulatory landscape for privacy coins.

talks.title: The Cost of Good Open Source Software
talks.teaser: Amir will answer questions about the Open Source Technology Improvement Fund (OSTIF), a nonprofit that help coordinate audits of open-source software and undertake other initiatives. OSTIF has helped Monero audit seve...
talks.summary:
In this talk at the DEF CON 27 Monero Village, Amir Montazery, managing director of the Open Source Technology Improvement Fund (OSTIF), discusses the economics and necessity of independent security audits for open-source digital infrastructure. He begins at 04:00 by illustrating how professional code reviews funded by OSTIF systematically discover and remediate critical security vulnerabilities, including the eradication of outdated cryptography algorithms, insecure dependencies, and unsafe third-party libraries across major privacy tools like OpenVPN, VeraCrypt, and WireGuard.

At 08:00, Amir shares concrete audit findings where code examinations uncovered severe denial-of-service vulnerabilities and entropy flaws in pseudo-random number generators (PRNGs), ensuring fixes were implemented before mainnet release. He highlights a marquee case study at 12:00: the comprehensive audit of Monero's Bulletproofs implementation, which independently verified zero-knowledge range proofs while shrinking transaction data sizes and miner fees by over eighty percent.

Turning to systemic open-source risks at 16:00, Amir explains that a single neglected sub-dependency can compromise an entire application stack despite robust top-level engineering. He details OSTIF's non-profit operational model at 20:00, showing how direct community sponsorships and corporate grants bridge the funding gap for volunteer-led software projects. He concludes at 24:00 by advocating for a collaborative ecosystem where security researchers, developers, and users collectively safeguard essential public software infrastructure. talks.title: Bulletproofs deep dive
talks.teaser: Bulletproofs are important zero-knowledge proofs used in Monero to hide transaction amounts, but they can be used to prove other statements too. Cathie will walk through many of these applications and constructions. T...
talks.summary:
Cathie Yun, a core contributor to the Rust Bulletproofs implementation, delivers an in-depth technical walkthrough of Bulletproofs—short non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs that operate without a trusted setup. Yun explains the mathematical foundations of Bulletproofs, their adoption in Monero to drastically reduce transaction sizes, and their broader utility for proving arbitrary statements.

[05:49] Yun explains the inner product argument at the heart of Bulletproofs, illustrating how vector commitments can be recursively split and folded in half each round. This folding technique shrinks proof sizes from linear O(N) down to logarithmic O(log N), allowing complex statements to be communicated and stored with minimal data overhead.

[15:46] The talk walks through the mechanics of range proofs, showing how Pedersen commitments and bit-decompositions prove that a confidential transaction value lies within a valid interval (such as [0, 2^64 - 1]) without revealing the underlying amount or causing balance overflows. Yun covers multi-proof aggregation [25:23], demonstrating how multiple range proofs can be batched together with logarithmic growth in proof size. Finally, she explains general constraint systems (R1CS) [38:40], showing how arithmetic circuits allow Bulletproofs to verify arbitrary relational logic and zero-knowledge smart contracts beyond simple range proofs.

talks.title: Encrypting the Web Isnt Enough
talks.teaser: Jeremy will be speaking about the EFF's past and ongoing efforts to encrypt the web.
talks.summary:
In this presentation at the DEF CON 27 Monero Village, Dr. Jeremy Gillula, Tech Projects Director at the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), explains why standard transport layer encryption like HTTPS is insufficient on its own to ensure comprehensive internet privacy. He opens by chronicling the widespread adoption of TLS across the web, highlighting at 09:00 how legacy mixed-content flaws historically leaked unencrypted HTTP assets such as images and tracking scripts. He reflects at 18:00 on how the EFF's Let's Encrypt initiative and automated Certbot tooling dramatically democratized certificate distribution globally.

However, Dr. Gillula emphasizes at 27:00 that TLS fails to conceal critical transaction metadata, specifically pointing out that unencrypted DNS lookups and plaintext Server Name Indication (SNI) headers broadcast the exact websites users visit to Internet Service Providers and network observers. He examines email protocols at 36:00, detailing how opportunistically encrypted STARTTLS connections are susceptible to downgrade and man-in-the-middle attacks, and explains how MTA-STS and TLSRPT provide cryptographic enforceability at 45:00.

Concluding with DNS privacy developments at 54:00, Dr. Gillula examines the technical tradeoffs and centralization risks of deploying DNS over HTTPS (DoH) through dominant cloud providers like Cloudflare. He argues that meaningful internet privacy demands the unified deployment of Encrypted SNI (ESNI), decentralized DNS resolvers, and metadata minimization across all communication layers. talks.title: Critical Role of Min Block Reward Trail Emission
talks.teaser: Francisco will provide an overview and review of blockchain scaling and fees in Monero. He will review the relationship between fees and the Cryptonote (now Monero) penalty with an emphasis on the impact of the block ...
talks.summary:
Francisco Cabañas examines the economic, cryptographic, and game-theoretic dynamics of proof-of-work blockchain scaling, focusing on the critical role of minimum block rewards (tail emission) and dynamic block sizes in Monero compared to Bitcoin's fixed-supply architecture.

[02:37] Cabañas breaks down Monero's dynamic block size algorithm, explaining how miners can expand block sizes to meet transaction demand but must pay a quadratic penalty on their block reward if the block exceeds the rolling median size. He details how rational miner behavior dictates transaction fees, demonstrating that transaction fees must remain proportional to block rewards so miners have an incentive to expand capacity only when transaction fees compensate for the lost reward penalty.

[13:28] The presentation contrasts this mechanism with Bitcoin's economic model, which caps total supply at 21 million and relies entirely on transaction fees to fund network security once block subsidies diminish. Cabañas highlights the systemic risks of a fee-only security model, including miner revenue instability, increased susceptibility to chain reorganizations, and selfish mining. He explains how Monero's perpetual tail emission of 0.6 XMR per block [21:58] guarantees a permanent baseline incentive for miners, ensuring robust network security while maintaining a predictable, disinflationary supply curve that drops below the historical inflation rate of gold.
